notes.title: Gamescom Update
notes.content: [p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45115665/425f45dd0daebd670363123b4ee0cf9cd3f3ed15.png"][/img][/p][p]It’s been a while since the last update due to the mentioned circumstances, but today we have a new build for you with some major changes and recent news. [/p][p]While we are working on sandbox mode and a new iteration of Ro.oTO a new progression system has been added and we changed the way of earning Data. Due to the new balancing of difficulty and progression we needed to reset all Hacker \[R]anking points. Bootcamp missions and settings stay as they are. We fixed many bugs and there are some other cool things to see.[/p][p]You highly requested a Wiki for Net.Attack() and we set up a page with the first pieces of information that can be used, filled and modified by you! Therefore we set up a new Discord channel if you have questions, feedback or any other wiki related issues. [url="https://netattack.wiki.gg/"]https://netattack.wiki.gg/[/url][/p][p]Net.Attack() can be played at the exhibition booth of ByteRockers' Games at Gamescom in Cologne. There will be some merch to grab and ROS!E is playable in the Daily Challenge again from August 20th to 24th not only at Gamecom, but also for everyone at home.   [/p][p][/p][p]We know you have been waiting for an update, and we are happy to finally upload a new build. Hopefully you’ll enjoy the changes! [/p][p]Have a nice Gamescom week and happy hacking![/p][p][/p][h1]Changes:[/h1][p][/p][h3]General:[/h3][list][*][p]Data is earned primarily through leveling up rather than by extracting chips[/p][list][*][p]Nodes and upgrades that worked with chip extraction have been adjusted[/p][/*][*][p]Tutorial rework along the new mechanic[/p][/*][/list][/*][*][p]New Mode “30Minute.Hack” available in difficulty selection → Play the Daily Challenge with your chosen character, region, and your progression[/p][/*][/list][list][*][p]Daily Challenge:[/p][list][*][p]Time is now limited to 30 minutes[/p][/*][*][p]The damage caused determines your ranking if you survive the 30 minutes[/p][/*][/list][/*][*][p]New destroyable object (Capacitor) in level that provides random rewards[/p][/*][*][p]Enemies have more variation in speed and knockback resistance[/p][/*][*][p]Save Game can be reset in the options (accessibility tab)[/p][/*][*][p]Updated Ingame Upgrades[/p][/*][*][p]There are new achievements to unlock[/p][/*][/list][h3]Metagame Progression:[/h3][list][*][p]New currency “Files (Ш)” can be earned via chip extraction[/p][/*][*][p]New menu “Dark Market” where “Files” can be exchanged[/p][/*][*][p]Balancing and difficulty has been adjusted[/p][/*][*][p]HackerRanking points had to be reset[/p][/*][/list][h3]Bugfixes:[/h3][list][*][p]Leveling every Ingame Upgrade no longer blocks the game[/p][/*][*][p]Select Nodes no longer kills the player under certain conditions[/p][/*][*][p]After a Bootcamp mission the code can be reviewed[/p][/*][*][p]Undo function caused false port connections[/p][/*][*][p]Some Root Nodes didn’t execute correctly[/p][/*][*][p]A bunch of text issues[/p][/*][*][p]Several other minor bugs[/p][/*][/list][h3]Known Issues:[/h3][list][*][p]Daily Challenge ranking display can differ in Run Summary and Daily Challenge screen.[/p][/*][/list]

notes.title: Net.Attack() Challenge Mode Demo Update
notes.content:
We’ve just released an update for Net.Attack() in which we added the new “Challenge Mode”. This will replace the Highscore Heist and is available from the main menu.

Your goal is still to survive as long as you can, but everyone gets the same character, level and the exact same nodes in the shop! These restrictions and your highscores are reset daily, so that you have 24 hours to prove your skills!

Changes:

[list]
[*] New Challenge Mode
[*] Balancing changes for Zu5el, difficulties, enemies
[*] Pings are making a lot more damage now
[*] Overclock no longer makes extra damage to the player
[*] The first two difficulty levels are now significantly easier
[*] Instead of node families be unlocked within a run, every node related to the chosen character can appear from the beginning now
[*] Bugfixes
[/list]

We are currently working on making Hop²a available to you again, so stay tuned and happy hacking!

notes.title: Net.Attack() Demo Update
notes.content:
Hey there,

thank you all for sticking with us as we’ve been working hard to further develop the game over the past few weeks, and welcome to all new Net.Attackers!

There has been so much valuable feedback and ideas showing your needs and wishes for the final game and we want to let you know how grateful we are.

Therefore we're excited to share the brand new version with you now and can’t wait to read your thoughts on your experience!

Changes:
[list]
[*] a bunch of new nodes
[*] balancing updates everywhere
[*] new enemies and wave behaviour
[*] Visible tag system for nodes
[*] Options for different screen resolutions
[*] general option functionality
[*] Big HUD mode
[*] improved node screen usability
[*] reworked character selection
[*] many new VFX and graphical improvements
[*] support for different coding conventions (PascalCase, kebab-case, camelCase, snake_case)
[/list]

Temporary Changes:
[list]
[*] The Highscore Heist mode is currently deactivated and will soon be replaced by a new Highscore system.
[*] Some Nodes are not available at the moment.
[*] Due to ongoing reworks only one character can be played.
[/list]

As some of you may have noticed, we did not participate in Steam Next Fest in February. This is due to some timetable changes that have to be made.

As we are back on track, we plan to provide you with regularly updated versions while we add more content to the game starting with this release.

Happy Hacking everyone and thanks for sharing your epic Net.Attack() moments - seeing this is the best thing for us!

[i]*Psst*[/i] You can also find a cheat code for the second level of the demo on our [url=https://discord.gg/BeDfDmKACR]Discord[/url] ;)

notes.title: Balancing an Unbalancable Game - Part 2
notes.content:
[h2]Feeling the Heat[/h2]
In this blog, I want to talk about a game system we implemented to better balance the gameplay—and why we ultimately decided to remove it: the heat system.

[h2]The Origins of the Heat System[/h2]
When Net.Attack() was just a game in my mind and I was experimenting with the first gameplay ideas, one thing quickly became apparent: balancing a game where players can code their own attacks would be incredibly challenging.

One of my first ideas to counteract the potentially overpowered nature of the system was something I called the Heat System. The concept was simple: every coding block would generate "heat" when executed. Heat would naturally reduce over time, but if executions generated too much heat, the player would overheat. An overheat would cancel all active code and freeze execution for five seconds. This forced players to optimize their code to avoid overheating. To balance this, we also included nodes that could reduce heat.

[h2]How It Worked[/h2]
Below is an example of the system in action. You can see the red numbers representing the heat generated by a node upon execution, and blue numbers showing the cooling effect (heat reduction).

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45115665/b09d22b015909e8344614a354b096fd5b9a61578.jpg[/img]

While the idea seemed reasonable at first, it quickly became clear that this system had significant drawbacks.

[h2]The Problems[/h2]
[olist]
[*] Difficulty Understanding the System Many players struggled to understand how the heat system worked. For instance, some assumed that if the numbers in their code resulted in a positive heat balance, they wouldn't overheat. However, that wasn't how it worked. Since each node’s execution generated heat, nodes that were executed multiple times in a single tick could easily generate more heat than expected. Explaining this mechanic proved challenging, especially for new players.
[*] The System Killed Creative Growth The heat system was designed to counteract exponential execution growth, but this also meant it heavily discouraged players from writing code that could escalate exponentially. As I mentioned in Part 1, that exponential growth is one of the most enjoyable aspects of the game.
[/olist]
I realized that I wanted the players' code to work as intended as often as possible. The heat mechanic often got in the way of creating truly great, creative solutions.


[h2]A Frustrating Player Experience[/h2]
A common scenario would go something like this:

[list]
[*] A player has an exciting idea: "I’ll connect these nodes, add a loop, and watch this escalate quickly!"
[*] The result: "Oh no, I overheated."
[/list]
This kind of experience was deeply unsatisfying. I wanted players to feel rewarded for their creativity, not punished by an obscure mechanic they didn’t fully understand.

[h2]The Decision to Let It Go[/h2]
In summary, the heat system did solve the problem it was designed for: it made the game more balanced and limited overpowered growth. But it came at a huge cost:
[list]
[*] It was difficult for beginners to understand.
[*] It often blocked players from executing their plans in frustrating and confusing ways.
[/list]
Ultimately, I decided to remove the heat system. Maybe it will rise again someday, but I honestly don’t think it will. The cost of restricting player creativity was simply too high.

Thank you for reading, and stay tuned for the next chapter in Balancing an Unbalancable Game!

notes.title: I want colour gradients! | Devblog #3
notes.content:
… is that one sentence my teammates hate meanwhile. Sometimes as an artist you come up with requests no other department can understand but you have a vision in mind and the unbreakable will to see it in your game! This is the old discussion about what needs to be done and what could be, but that’s another story.

[h3]Why colour gradients?[/h3]

For me adding gradients is a cheap way to modify a scenes mood and colour, similar to lighting. It adds detail where is none and can improve the visual impression without affecting the assets itself. Therefore it is absolutely not necessary that this effect can be actively be noticed by the player, otherwise it can be disturbing while playing.  It's more about a kind of feeling that will be missed if turned off - the “certain something”.

To give you an idea what it looks like,  have a close look at these comparison pictures.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45115665/681eef50aa9d0b99c74de115cb09b85655fa4483.png[/img]

For Net.Attack() we not only added it to the game scene but also to every User Interface:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45115665/cc907cb86701c996be8f1d02ea3cb6e19a704f8d.png[/img]

In some cases it can be useful to strengthen the effect with the intention to connect the different asset colours a little bit more and harmonize the overall look.

[h3]How I got them (or any other “fancy” art feature)[/h3]

Besides from including ideas into backlog, I always try to mention features that I want to have seen implemented whenever I get the chance. Especially when there is a time spot for “Nice to haves”, after builds are done or the team is in the mood of “adding something cool”. That’s the first way it won’t be forgotten in the deeps of the backlog.

By knowing that the ones who i want working time from can not truly imagine what I have in mind, it is important to make sure they will understand what there is to win. Therefore I try to show modified screenshots, concepts and references. If you’re lucky you have that one passionate technical artist who supports your vision with convincing hacky solutions directly in game.

On the long run I gained the trustment from the team that my ideas are not completely that crazy art stuff no other human can appreciate and that I myself priorise what is worth the efford. Achieving this is the best!
